The ostensible reason given is, that Berodach Baladan had heard of Hezekiah’s illness, and therefore sent to congratulate him on his recovery; but in <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.31">2Ch 32:31</reference> the further reason is mentioned, that he wished to inquire concerning the miracle upon the sun-dial. But, as Josephus has shown, the true object, no doubt, was to make sure of Hezekiah’s friendship in anticipation of his intended revolt from the Assyrian rule. <hi type="italic">Berodach Baladan</hi>, for <hi type="italic">Merodach Baladan</hi> (Isa.), with the labial changed, is the same person as the <hi type="italic">Marodach Baladan</hi> who reigned in Babylon for six months, according to Alex. Polyhistor, or rather Berosus (Euseb. <hi type="italic">Chr. armen</hi>. i. pp. 42, 43), and was slain by <hi type="italic">Elibus</hi>, and also the same as the <hi type="italic">Mardokempad</hi> who reigned, according to the <hi type="italic">Can. Ptol</hi>., from 26 to 38 <hi type="italic">aer. Nab.</hi>, i.e., from 721 to 709 b.c. The first part of the name, מרדך, occurs in <reference osisRef="Jer.50.2">Jer 50:2</reference> in connection with <hi type="italic">Bel</hi> as the name of a Babylonian idol; and the whole name is found on a cylinder (in the British Museum) which contains the first expeditions of Sennacherib against Babylon and Media, and upon the inscriptions at Khorsabad spelt either <hi type="italic">Merodak-pal-dsana</hi> (according to Brandis, <hi type="italic">Ueber der Gewinn</hi>, pp. 44 and 53) or <hi type="italic">Marduk bal iddin</hi> (according to Oppert).<note placement="foot">Compare M. v. Niebuhr, <hi type="italic">Gesch. Ass.</hi> p. 40; and with regard to the chronological differences, on account of which many have called in question the identity of Merodach Baladan either with the <hi type="italic">Marudach-Baladan</hi> of Berosus or with the <hi type="italic">Mardokempad</hi> of the <hi type="italic">Can. Ptol.</hi>, see the discussion of this point at pp. 75ff.</note> <div eID="gen5437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5438" type="x-p"/> Instead of שׁמע כּי we have ויּשׁמע in Isaiah, which is not so clear, though it is probably more original; whereas the clause in Isaiah, ויּחזק חלה כּי, “that he had been sick and had become strengthened, i.e., well again,” is simply an elucidation of the הזקיּהוּ חלה כּי of our text, in which the recovery is implied in the pluperfect “had been sick.”
entries.855ccf8bff3c00f4459cd326b57be988acf89b32: 2Ki 20:20-21 <div eID="gen5442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5443" type="x-p"/> Close of Hezekiah’s reign. - On the basin (בּרכח) and the aqueduct constructed by him, see at 2Ki 18:17.  <chapter eID="2Kgs.20"/> <div eID="gen5443" type="x-p"/>

                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Give charge con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning thine house.</ns0:note> Set thine house in order <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Take care to make thy Will, and to settle the Affairs of thy Family and Kingdom: which he the rather presseth upon him, because the state of his Kingdom required it: for it is plain, that <ns0:hi>Hezekiah</ns0:hi> had not as yet any Son, <ns0:hi>Manasseh</ns0:hi> his Heir and Successor not being born till three Years after this time, by comparing this <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 20. 6. with <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 21. 1.</ns0:note>: for thou shalt die, and not live <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">According to the course of Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture, and of thy Disease, which is mortal in its kind, and will be so in effect, if God doth not miraculously prevent it.                   <ns0:p n="2">2 Th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>n he turned his face to the wall <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Either, because the Temple lay that way: or rather, that by turning his Face from the company, he might inti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mate his desire of privacy, and so might with more freedom and fervency pour out his Soul to God.</ns0:note>, and prayed unto the LORD, saying,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 I beseech thee, O LORD, remember now how I have walked before thee in truth <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Sincerely, with an honest mind, as the following words explain it. I have in some measure (humane frailty excepted) kept the condition which thou didst require, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 8. 25. and therefore do humbly beg of thee, that the Promise made to <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> and to his Posterity upon that con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dition, may not fail in my Person, for as yet thou hast not given me a Son. See on <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 1. I am not conscious to my self of any gross exorbitancies in the course of my life, for which thou usest to shorten mens days, and cut off my life in thy displeasure, which by this sharp Message thou threat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nest to do.</ns0:note>, and with a perfect heart, and have done <ns0:hi>that which is</ns0:hi> good in thy sight: and Hezekiah wept <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> with a great weep<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing.</ns0:note> sore <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Partly, for that horror of death which is and was common to men, especially, in the times of the <ns0:hi>Old Testament,</ns0:hi> when the Grace of God in Christ was not so ful<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly manifested, as now it is: and principally, for the distra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cted and miserable condition in which the Church and State were then likely to be left, through the uncertainty of the Succession to the Crown, and the great proneness of the Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple to backslide to their false worship, and evil practises; which he easily perceived, and which he knew would bring far worse Calamities upon them, if he were removed; as af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terwards it came to pass.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And it came to pass, afore Isaiah was gone out into the middle <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">

Or, <ns0:hi>into the middle city,</ns0:hi> as it is in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew.</ns0:hi> For some observe, that there were three Cities, or three parts of this City; one called <ns0:hi>the city of David</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Sion;</ns0:hi> another <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> led <ns0:hi>Iebus,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Salem;</ns0:hi> and a third which was betwixt these two parts, and united them all into one City, called <ns0:hi>Ierusa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lem.</ns0:hi> This is noted to shew Gods great readiness to hear the sincere and fervent prayers of his Children.</ns0:note>, that the word of the LORD came to him, saying,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:320" />5 Turn again, and tell Hezekiah the captain of my people, Thus saith the LORD, the God of Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid thy father <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">I am mindful of my Promise made to <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> and his House, and will make it good in thy Person.</ns0:note>, I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will heal thee; on the third day <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Which shews that the cure was Miraculous.</ns0:note> thou shalt go up into the house of the LORD <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">To give me Solemn Praise for this Mercy. Which proves the perfection of the cure.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And I will add unto thy days fifteen years <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Beyond what thou dost expect, and beyond what thou wouldst do if I should leave thee to the force of thy Disease.</ns0:note>, and I will deliver thee and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">This is added, either, first, Because he might otherwise fear the <ns0:hi>Assyrians</ns0:hi> return to this City from which he was so shamefully repulsed. Or, Secondly, Because this sickness hap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pened before that great slaughter, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 19. 35. Of which see the Notes on <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 1.</ns0:note>: and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 19. 34.</ns0:note> I will defend this city for mine own sake <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To vindicate my Glory against that insolent Blasphemer.</ns0:note>, and for my servant Davids sake.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And Isaiah said, Take a lump of figs <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Though the deliverance was certainly Promised, yet means must be used, and those suitable: for this hath na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />turally a power of ripening and softning Boils or Sores; though that power was altogether insufficient to produce so sudden and so compleat a Cure.</ns0:note>. And they took and laid <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> on the boil <ns0:note place="bottom">Which seems to have been a Plague-sore.</ns0:note>, and he reco<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vered.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 ¶ And Hezekiah said <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Or rather, <ns0:hi>had said:</ns0:hi> for it is evident this was said be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore his recovery, though his recovery be mentioned before it; such transpositions being frequent in Scripture.</ns0:note> unto Isaiah, What <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> the sign <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">He asketh a sign, not because he distrusted it; but for the strengthning of his Faith, which otherwise might be shaken by the greatness of his danger, and by the contradiction be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tween this and his former Message. Compare <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 6. 17, 37, 39. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 7. 11.</ns0:note> that the LORD will heal me, and that I shall go up into the house of the LORD the third day?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And Isaiah said, This sign shalt thou have of the LORD, that the LORD will do the thing that he hath spoken: shall the shadow go forward ten degrees, or go back ten degrees?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And Hezekiah answered, It is a light thing for the shadow to go down ten degrees <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">To wit, in an instant: for that course or motion of the Sun is natural for the kind of it, though miraculous for the swiftness of it; but the other would be both ways miracu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lous.</ns0:note>: nay, but let the shadow return backward ten degrees.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And Isaiah the prophet cried unto the LORD <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Being moved by Gods Spirits first to offer him this sign, and then to pray for it.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 38. 8.</ns0:note> he brought the shadow ten degrees backward <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> 1. What were these <ns0:hi>degrees? Ans.</ns0:hi> Lines in the Dial: but whether each of these Lines or Degrees noted an hour, or half an hour, or a quarter of an hour, is uncertain, and not very considerable in this case. <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> 2. What was it that went down? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> Either, First, The Shadow alone went back without the Sun. For God could so dispose of the Light of the Sun, by interposing Clouds or other things, so that the Shadow should fall onely upon those Lines, and in that manner as God directed it. And whereas the <ns0:hi>sun</ns0:hi> is said to have gone down, that may be spoken according to appearance, as other passages of Scri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pture are understood, as when the Moon is called one of the <ns0:hi>great lights,</ns0:hi> Gen. 1. though it be less than some of the Stars: and when <ns0:hi>the sun</ns0:hi> is said to <ns0:hi>go down,</ns0:hi> Jer. 15. 9. and to be <ns0:hi>turned into darkness,</ns0:hi> Joel 2. 31. Or, Secondly, The Sun it self went back, and the Shadow with it. This may seem most probable: First, By comparing this with <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 10. 13. where the Sun it self stood still. Secondly, Because it is said, <ns0:hi>the sun</ns0:hi> it self <ns0:hi>returned,</ns0:hi> Isa. 38. 8. for which he here menti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons <ns0:hi>the shadow</ns0:hi> onely, because the Miracle was not so easily discovered in the Sun, as in the Shadow of a Dial. And though <ns0:hi>the sun</ns0:hi> may be elsewhere taken improperly, yet where the improper signification is unnecessary, the proper is and ought to be preferred before it. Thirdly, Because this Miracle was noted by the <ns0:hi>Babylonians,</ns0:hi> who, having un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood that it was done for <ns0:hi>Hezekiah</ns0:hi> his sake, sent to en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quire into the truth and manner of it, 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 32. 31. <ns0:hi>Obj.</ns0:hi> If this had been done, the Heathen Historians and Astrono<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mers would have taken notice of it, which we do not find that they did. <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> So it is most probable they did: al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />though those Books be not now extant: which is not strange; this being confessed and bewailed, that so very few of the first and Ancient Writers are now left. <ns0:hi>Herodotus</ns0:hi> himself, the first, and Father of the ancient Historians, being long after this time. And yet it is observed, that there are some inti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mations of these things left, though mixed with fables, as many true Histories were; as what the Poets fabled of <ns0:hi>Iu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />piter</ns0:hi>'s making the Night twice as long as it should have been, that he might enjoy <ns0:hi>Al<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>mena</ns0:hi> longer. Whether the Sun or Sha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dow went backward suddenly, or leisurely, and in the same time in which it had gone down, is a question of no great moment, the Miracle being evident either way.</ns0:note>, by which it had gone down in the <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> degrees.</ns0:note> dial of Ahaz <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Which <ns0:hi>A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />haz</ns0:hi> had made in the Kings Palace. This Dial he mentions, because the truth of the Miracle might be best and soonest discovered there; this Dial possibly being visible out of the Kings Chamber, or at least beingnear to it, and the De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />grees be ing most distinct and conspicuous in this Dial; but the same thing was discerned by all other Dials.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> At that time Berodach baladan <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Called <ns0:hi>Berodach-baladan,</ns0:hi> Isa. 39. 1. whose name <ns0:hi>Iose<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phus</ns0:hi> found in that famous <ns0:hi>Chaldaean</ns0:hi> Historian, <ns0:hi>Berosus.</ns0:hi> He seems to have been the King of <ns0:hi>Assyria</ns0:hi>'s Vice-Roy in <ns0:hi>Baby<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lon,</ns0:hi> and upon that terrible slaughter of 185 thousand in the <ns0:hi>Assyrian</ns0:hi> Host, and the death of <ns0:hi>Sennacherib,</ns0:hi> and the dif<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ferences among his Sons, to have usurped an absolute So<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vereignty over <ns0:hi>Babylon;</ns0:hi> and either himself or his Son de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stroyed the <ns0:hi>Assyrian</ns0:hi> Monarchy, and translated the Empire to <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi>
